 ONE Championship: Rodtang faces fresh questions but Nong-O backs him to rise again 
 Former flyweight champion says he will fight on after a second straight defeat, with old rival Tenshin Nasukawa among those offering support
 PUBLISHED : 15 Nov 2026 at 16:45
 WRITER: 
 Nick Atkin 
 Listen 
   Small 
   Medium 
   Large 
 Share
 Facebook
 Reddit
 Copy Link
 Nong-O (right) kneels and clasps Rodtang’s gloves as he consoles him after the fight 
 Rodtang Jitmuangnon was left in tears again, this time on the canvas at Lumpinee Stadium.
 Nong-O Hama, who had just beaten him in ONE Championship’s flyweight Muay Thai Grand Prix, knelt beside him to console him.
 They embraced and talked after the final bell. When Nong-O got up, Rodtang stayed a little longer, both hands down and his head bowed.
 The judges gave Nong-O a unanimous decision in Friday’s quarter-final at The Inner Circle 38, a second-round head-kick knockdown putting an emphatic stamp on the win. 
 It was Rodtang’s second straight defeat, and it arguably raises even more questions than his fifth-round stoppage by Takeru Segawa in April, when he was dropped four times.
 A cut opened by Nong-O’s elbow is visible above Rodtang’s swollen left eye after the bout
 If there were doubts about the “Iron Man’s” chin after Tokyo, another knockdown in his own sport has only sharpened them.
 British Muay Thai veteran Liam Harrison recalled seeing Rodtang take the same kick from Jonathan Haggerty, shake it off and throw back a combination.
 “This time was always gonna come when that invincibility ran out,” Harrison wrote on X. “Be interesting to see where he goes from here.”
 In the photo Rodtang posted on Facebook, one eye was swollen almost shut and a line of stitches ran through the cut above it, courtesy of a slicing elbow from Nong-O. 
 “To all my beloved fans, I’m truly sorry for letting you down. I gave it everything I had. I feel deeply disappointed and heartbroken,” he wrote.
 “But if my fans still want me to keep fighting, I’ll be ready to fight again for every single one of you who still loves and believes in me.”
 Nong-O (right) catches Rodtang with a left high kick in the second round
 Tenshin Nasukawa, who needed an extra round to beat Rodtang for the RISE featherweight title in 2018, replied to the same post on Instagram. 
 “That’s just how life is sometimes. You know I’ll always be cheering you on, bro,” the Japanese icon told him.
 By Saturday, Rodtang had made up his mind. “I’ve thought it over. I’ll keep going for the fans who love me,” he wrote in a follow-up Facebook post reported by Khaosod.
 Asked at Lumpinee on Friday whether Rodtang could become champion again, the man who had just beaten him was certain.
 “A hundred per cent,” Nong-O told the Bangkok Post. “If he still keeps going.”
 There had been tears in Tokyo, too. Rodtang wept in his corner after the kickboxing rematch at ONE Samurai 1.
 A cut opened by Nong-O’s elbow is visible above Rodtang’s swollen left eye after the bout
 He had knocked out Takeru in 80 seconds in their first meeting the previous year. Takeru avenged that loss in his retirement fight and left with the interim flyweight kickboxing title.
 The build-up to that fight came amid a bitter contract dispute with ONE that had spilled into the courts.
 At the post-event press conference, ONE boss Chatri Sityodtong took an apparent swipe at Rodtang, while praising Haggerty’s discipline. “I think we saw what happens when you make a lot of money and fame gets to your head,” he said.
 Rodtang signed a new deal in July, when ONE Thailand president Jitinat “Plai” Asdamongkol said the promotion and Jitmuangnon Gym had a plan to rebuild him.
 In his public apology after signing, Rodtang said he had cut ties with people he felt had led him astray. The old Iron Man, he told fans, was back.
 The Grand Prix gave him a way back to the Muay Thai title he lost on the scales in November 2024, before beating Jacob Smith by unanimous decision.
 Rodtang roars in his corner before his ONE Championship flyweight Muay Thai Grand Prix quarter-final
 At his open workout in Nonthaburi, the 29-year-old said he had spent nearly two months in camp. “I’m in much better physical condition than I was for my last fight,” he said.
 His nutritionist said he had stuck to his training and diet plans. Rodtang made weight and passed hydration with no issues on Thursday. This time he’d had the sort of camp he had lacked in April.
 Nong-O, a Thai legend who had turned 40 just three days earlier, gave him a chance to show what that work had done.
 Rodtang had grown up watching Nong-O and compared the fight to testing his skills against a teacher. “Whatever the result, once we leave the ring we’re still brothers,” he said at the workout.
 He pressed forward and worked the body early on Friday. In the second round, Nong-O cut him badly with an elbow and put him down with a left head kick.
 Rodtang Jitmuangnon bows his head on the canvas after losing to Nong-O Hama at Lumpinee Stadium
 Rodtang, somehow, beat the count and went straight back after him. He was still pressing for a finish in the third as Nong-O tied him up in the clinch, but the clock was against him.
 It is Nong-O who now moves on to face Shimon Yoshinari in the Grand Prix, with the flyweight world title also at play in the final.
 Rodtang’s old belt has rarely looked further away. He entered the night ranked No 2, a place above Nong-O, and may now have to rebuild against someone further down the division.
 Who he faces next is anyone’s guess, but Ramadan Ondash – whom Shimon beat in Friday’s other quarter-final – could be a good test.
 Rodtang won’t need to look far for guidance – Nong-O has had to pick himself up more than once.
 He had defended his bantamweight belt seven times before Jonathan Haggerty took it with a first-round KO in 2023. Asadula Imangazaliev left him out cold in March, ending his bid for the then-vacant flyweight title. Three months later, Nong-O was back at Lumpinee, beating Kongthoranee Sor Sommai to settle their trilogy. He still went into the Rodtang fight a 7-2 outsider.
 “We lose, OK, it doesn’t matter,” Nong-O said when asked about his own chances of becoming champion again. “I’m happy when I fight.”
 On the canvas, he had told Rodtang to put this one behind him.
 “There’s always a new beginning,” Nong-O said through an interpreter. “So he can start again.”
